Mathematical modeling research

The novel coronavirus disease (COVID-19), caused by the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), in Africa is characterized by asymptomatic (or mildly symptomatic) individuals who are believed to play a role in the spread of the disease.
The extent and position of the lesion in individuals with asymptomatic conditions are not easily detectable.
Our study shows that their monitoring is crucial for the containment of the spread of SARS-CoV-2.

A deterministic mathematical model, the susceptible-exposed-infectious-removed (SEIR) model, was developed to assess the impact of asymptomatic individuals on the spread of SARS-CoV-2, but with a focus on the control of transmission in the Lusaka region of Zambia.
In modeling for two scenarios; (1) predicting that asymptomatic individuals account for 70% of COVID-19 cases and (2) asymptomatic individuals account for only 50% of the cases.

For comparison, the model was evaluated under the assumption that asymptomatic individuals are as infectious as those showing symptoms and secondly, assuming that asymptomatic individuals are less infectious than those showing symptoms.

For a model considering a 70% asymptomatic infection rate, a daily blanket testing of ≥ 7911 tests/100000 population is required to prevent the spread of the disease if asymptomatic individuals are to be isolated when symptomatic individuals are expected to undergo testing ≥ 10028 tests/100000 population.

For 50% asymptomatic individuals, a minimum blanket testing of ≥ 4540 tests/100000 population is required to prevent the spread at both levels of transmission from asymptomatic individuals to those showing symptoms.

Our model predicts that the differential diagnosis of COVID-19, which includes asymptomatic individuals, through blanket screening could be used as a measure to curb the spread of SARS-CoV-2 in Lusaka, Zambia, but its cost will be high.

In some parts of Africa and Asia, female genital mutilation (FGM), also known as 'cutting of the female genitalia,' is still practiced.
